strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing long-horizon decision-making under partial observability with clear presentation and intuitive examples

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three diverse benchmarks (T-Maze, MIKASA-Robo, POPGym-48) showing consistent improvements and strong results (100% T-Maze success at 1M steps, ~2× improvement on manipulation)
Formal theoretical analysis characterizing LRU memory dynamics with exponential forgetting bounds and memory boundedness guarantees (Propositions 1-2)
Computational efficiency: faster per-step inference than strong baselines (RATE, DT) despite improved performance
Thorough experimental protocol with proper error bars, multiple runs, detailed ablations, and complete hyperparameter disclosure for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (external memory, LRU replacement, cross-attention) without fundamental innovations; DeepSeek-MoE FFN choice appears orthogonal and ablation shows MLP equivalence
Scope restricted to offline imitation learning—no online RL, exploration, or environments with reinforcement signals, limiting applicability and impact for an RL paper
Claims about 'real-world robotics' contradicted by exclusive focus on simulation; no real robot deployments despite framing and motivation suggesting practical robotic applications

Overstated horizon extension claims: T-Maze 100,000× extension conflates context length with genuine reasoning complexity; task is trivial once single-bit cue is stored; large gap between theoretical bounds and empirical horizons unexplained

Severe hyperparameter sensitivity: task-specific tuning required (memory size: 2-256, λ: 0.05-0.9, context: 10-60 tokens); Figure 6 shows instability at intermediate λ; no principled guidance for new tasks

Weak theoretical-practical connection: theory assumes bounded updates without analyzing guarantees; effective horizon formula H(ε) diverges significantly from practice; no analysis of information retention or cross-attention access mechanisms

Ablations limited to RememberColor3-v0, a task where baseline methods achieve near-perfect scores, limiting informativeness; shared memory ablation (0.45 vs 1.0) suggests ablation task is too easy; missing ablations on harder variants
No mechanistic analysis: lack of memory embedding visualization, access pattern analysis, or investigation of learned representations; unclear what information model explicitly decides to store

Mixed and modest MIKASA-Robo improvements on some tasks (RememberColor5: 0.13→0.19, RememberColor9: 0.09→0.23) with only 3 runs; statistical significance testing absent; POPGym shows inconsistent gains and some task underperformance

Missing comparisons with recent memory-augmented architectures (xLSTM, structured state-space models); detached segment gradients limit credit assignment; design choices lack justification (reversed relative bias, memory initialization)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse benchmarks (T-Maze, MIKASA-Robo, POPGym) with extensive baselines and thorough ablation studies
Outstanding memory probing analysis (Section A.9, Figures 9-15) that provides concrete evidence the model uses memory functionally rather than relying on parameter count
Strong empirical results on target domain: ~70% improvement over RATE on MIKASA-Robo and 100% success on T-Maze up to 1M steps
Formal theoretical analysis of memory dynamics with exponential forgetting bounds and retention horizon characterization
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, procedures, and promised code release
Practical efficiency gains despite modest parameter increase, enabled by bounded memory design
Perfect generalization across T-Maze train/test length distributions (Figure 4)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing components (external memory, cross-attention, LRU, MoE-FFN) without fundamental innovation
Severely restricted scope: limited to imitation learning in simulation with no online RL or real robot experiments, significantly limiting applicability claims
Critical hyperparameter sensitivity without principled selection methods: memory size M and blending λ are highly task-dependent (Figure 6, Table 7) with no guidance for new domains

Mixed experimental results undermine generalization claims: underperformance on ViZDoom navigation (55.28 vs 59.21 RATE), only modest gains on POPGym reactive tasks (9.2 vs 9.1), and comparable performance on D4RL MDPs
Theoretical analysis is relatively straightforward and doesn't explain why ELMUR works empirically or characterize actual sample complexity; gap between theory and practice remains unclear

Memory mechanism design choices lack justification: per-layer memory shows dramatic failure with sharing (0.45 vs 1.0) but this may be a design artifact; no ablations on segment detachment or convex blending alternatives
Some baseline results appear surprisingly weak (DT gets 0.01±0.01 on RememberColor3) raising possible implementation concerns; limited comparison with other long-context approaches
High variance on some tasks with no statistical significance testing; some improvements within error bounds
